threads.thread_goal: Align on incident scenarios, scope, and playbook structure.

messages.text:
Kicking off the Crisis Communication Playbook for On-site Security Incidents project (project_pack_ref: Crisis Communication Playbook). Our goal over the next three weeks is to get a usable v1 in place before the next quarterly safety drill.
For this thread, can we align on: 1) the 4–6 priority incident scenarios to cover in v1, and 2) the overall structure and section owners for the playbook.
I suggest we use T1 to map scenarios and gaps, and T2 to lock the structure and ownership. A8 will help us keep roles and contacts straight.
First question: which incident types do you see as must-have for v1 based on what you have seen on site and in past comms situations

From a PR and newsroom perspective, the incidents that usually trigger external attention are:
- Physical altercation or assault on site
- Fire or suspected fire / smoke event
- Bomb threat or suspicious package
- Major medical emergency (e.g. collapse, serious injury)
- Police activity on or around the site
These map well to T1 and give us five clear buckets. We can add a sixth for prolonged service disruption if operations think it is needed.
For structure in T2, I would start with: incident overview, on-site escalation, internal updates, external/media handling, post-incident review. We can then map owners using A8 so there is no confusion during an incident.

From the guard side, the ones we actually see and call in most often are:
- Fights or aggressive behaviour at entrances or in parking areas
- Fire alarms going off, sometimes false, sometimes real smoke
- Suspicious bags or boxes left in corridors or near exits
- People getting hurt on stairs or loading docks
- Police showing up asking for CCTV or access
These line up with what 143124 listed. I would keep it to five for now so the checklist and scripts stay short enough to use under stress.
For T1 I can help describe what we currently do on the radio and who we call first, but I will need support to phrase it clearly for the playbook.

From a training and staff understanding angle, five scenarios feels like the upper limit for v1 if we want people to actually remember the flows.
I would group them as:
1) Violence or aggressive behaviour
2) Fire or smoke
3) Suspicious object or threat
4) Serious medical emergency
5) Police or emergency services on site
This gives us a clean structure for briefings and exercises later.
For T2, I suggest we mirror that grouping in the table of contents and keep a consistent pattern per scenario so frontline staff can recognise the layout quickly.

Agree with the five scenarios proposed. From a community relations angle, police activity and anything that looks like a fire tend to generate the most questions from neighbours and local media.
I would keep prolonged service disruption as a later addition unless operations insists, otherwise we risk diluting focus in v1.
On T2, I can co-own the external/media handling sections with 143124, and also take the lead on aligning with community priorities later via T11.
We should capture these owner assignments in A8 so that on-site teams know who to call for which part.

Thanks, this is helpful context.
To move toward a decision on scope: does anyone see a critical incident type missing from the five we have on the table: violence, fire/smoke, suspicious object or threat, serious medical emergency, police or emergency services on site
If not, I propose we lock these as the v1 focus for T1 and T2, and treat service disruption as a candidate for v1.1.
On structure, here is a strawman for T2:
- Section 1: Overview and principles (owner: 286680)
- Section 2: Incident scenarios and on-site escalation (owner: 47290 with support)
- Section 3: Internal staff updates (owner: 47537)
- Section 4: External/media handling (owners: 143124 and 409854)
- Section 5: Stakeholder and contact matrix (owner: 143124, based on A8)
- Section 6: Post-incident review and updates (owner: 143124, linked to T10 later)
Please flag any concerns before we confirm.

The five scenarios work for me, and they match what we usually see in media coverage.
On the structure, I would only tweak Section 5 slightly: I can own the initial draft of the stakeholder and contact matrix in A8, but we should have operations validate it before we rely on it in a live situation.
Otherwise, I am comfortable being listed as owner for Sections 4, 5, and 6 in T2, with 409854 co-owning the external/media handling part.
If no one objects, we can record these five scenarios as the v1 scope and move on to filling T1 with current handling steps and gaps.

No objections from my side. The five scenarios are also easy to explain in training and to use as modules.
For Section 3 in T2, I will focus on short, plain-language internal updates that managers can deliver verbally or by email, and we can later connect that to A4.
Happy to be listed as owner for that section. I will also keep an eye on how the structure will translate into T5 and T6 so we do not have to rework later.

I am ok with the five scenarios. They match what we actually face.
For Section 2 in T2, I can start by writing out what guards do now for each scenario, step by step, including who we call on the radio and when we contact police or fire services. Someone will need to help me adjust the wording so it fits the playbook style.
I will also check that what we write does not conflict with the legal and safety rules we already follow on site, especially around fire safety and when we can use force.

Fine with the five scenarios and with the owner list you proposed.
On Section 4 in T2, I will focus on making sure our external messages are consistent and sensitive to local community concerns, and that they can be easily approved by legal and senior management.
I will coordinate with 143124 so that A3 and A5 later reflect the same structure and scenario naming as T2.

Sounds like we have convergence.
To capture it explicitly: v1 of the playbook will cover five priority incident scenarios: 1) violence or aggressive behaviour, 2) fire or smoke, 3) suspicious object or threat, 4) serious medical emergency, and 5) police or emergency services on site.
We will use the six-section structure outlined in T2, with owners as discussed: 286680 for overview, 47290 for on-site escalation, 47537 for internal updates, 143124 and 409854 for external/media, 143124 for stakeholder matrix and post-incident review, with operations validating A8.
I will update T1 and T2 to reflect this and share a short summary in A1 once we have first drafts.
If anyone sees a gap, please flag it today so we can still adjust before we start drafting in detail.

Thanks for summarising. I will start filling T1 for the media and stakeholder angle, focusing on current gaps in how we coordinate with on-site teams and how quickly we can get a holding line out.
Once we have that, it will be easier to design the external sections in T2 and later A3 and A5.
Please tag me when the first guard-side steps for each scenario are written so I can check for any communication blind spots.

I will translate the agreed structure into a simple outline for internal briefings so that when we get to T5 and T6 we are not reinventing the flow.
Once T1 has the current steps and gaps, I can also highlight where staff understanding tends to break down and what we should emphasise in training.
I will share a first outline for the internal updates section in T2 by tomorrow.

I will start writing the current steps for each of the five scenarios into T1 this afternoon, focusing on what guards actually do now.
I might need someone to review the wording so it is clear enough for the playbook, but I can at least get the sequence and who we call down on paper.
Once that is in, we can see where the gaps are and what needs to change for the new scripts.

threads.thread_goal: Define on-site escalation scripts and quick-reference checklists.

messages.text:
I have put a first draft of the on-site escalation steps into T3 for the five scenarios we agreed.
It is basically what guards do now, written as short steps: who we call on the radio, when we hit the fire alarm, when we call police or ambulance, and when we inform the site manager.
Before we turn this into the On-site Incident Escalation Checklist in A2 and the one-pagers in T8, can you please review if the order and wording make sense and if anything important is missing
I want to be sure this is clear enough for guards to follow quickly during an incident.

Thanks for getting the first draft into T3.
I have gone through the steps for violence, fire/smoke, and suspicious object. The sequence mostly matches what we want, but I see a few places where we should be more explicit about when to prioritise life safety over information gathering, and when to stop engaging and wait for police.
For A2 and T8, I suggest we:
- Keep each scenario to a single column of short, numbered steps
- Use clear triggers like 'if there is visible smoke' or 'if a weapon is seen'
- Add a simple reminder about preserving CCTV and not sharing details with bystanders or media
I will propose a revised layout for A2 based on your content and share a screenshot later today for feedback.

I have read through the T3 draft as well, focusing on clarity for people who may be under stress.
A few suggestions:
- Use very simple verbs: 'call', 'move', 'wait', 'inform'
- Avoid long conditional sentences; break them into separate steps
- For each scenario, add a short 'do not' box at the bottom (for example, do not share photos, do not speculate about causes)
This will make it easier to turn T3 into A2 and the printed checklists in T8, and it will also align with the language we use in training later.
Once we agree on the wording, I can help test the script with a couple of staff members to see if anything is confusing.

From a PR angle, the main thing I look for in T3 and A2 is that nothing in the on-site script conflicts with what we will later say externally.
Two points to check:
- For suspicious objects and threats, we should avoid any language that could be interpreted as confirming a bomb or similar until authorities have assessed the situation.
- For incidents with injuries, we should be clear that only designated people speak to families or media, and that guards refer any questions to them.
If we add a short line in each scenario in A2 about who handles external questions, it will help avoid mixed messages later when we use A3.

Agree with 143124. I would also add a simple reminder in A2 that any social media posts about the incident must come from the official channels only, not from personal accounts.
For T8, maybe we can include a small footer on each one-page checklist with the name or role of the person authorised to speak externally.
This will support the multi-channel strategy we are building in A5 and T7 and reduce the risk of conflicting messages.

I have updated T3 with shorter steps and added the 'do not' boxes as suggested.
For example, in the violence scenario I changed it to: 1) Move to a safe distance if possible, 2) Call control on the radio, 3) If there is a weapon, do not try to disarm, 4) Call police, 5) Inform site manager.
Can you check if this fits the layout you have in mind for A2 and T8 I want to be sure we are not missing any legal or safety points before we say this is final.

I have reviewed your latest T3 updates. The steps are much clearer now.
I have translated the five scenarios into a draft A2 checklist with one page per scenario and a consistent structure: triggers, immediate actions, who to inform, what not to do.
Before we call A2 final, I would like one more check from 47537 on readability and from 143124 on any wording that might cause issues if it is later quoted or leaked.
Assuming no major changes, I propose we treat this version of A2 as the final content for v1 and move on to formatting and distribution.

I have gone through the A2 draft. The language is simple enough for frontline staff, and the structure is consistent across scenarios.
I made a few small edits to remove double negatives and to keep verbs at the start of each step, but nothing that changes the meaning.
From my side, I am comfortable treating this as the v1 content for the on-site escalation checklist, and we can refine after we test it in training and drills.

I have checked A2 from a reputational and legal risk angle.
The wording avoids confirming causes or labels like bomb, and it clearly directs staff not to speak to media or post on social channels. That aligns with what we plan for A3 and A5.
I do not see anything that would create problems if the checklist were photographed or shared externally.
I support closing A2 as the v1 content, with the understanding that legal and safety teams will still do a final review as part of T3 and T8.

Great, with both of your reviews, we can record that the v1 content of the on-site incident escalation checklist in A2 is approved for this project phase.
Next question is how we make A2 and the T8 one-pagers available on site.
My suggestion is both print and digital: printed copies in control rooms and at key posts, plus a mobile-friendly PDF accessible via QR code or the intranet. That way we are covered if printers fail or if someone is away from the desk.
Any concerns with this mixed approach

From the guard side, we definitely need printed copies in the control room and maybe laminated versions at some posts.
Phones are not always allowed on the floor, and in some areas the signal is bad, so we cannot rely only on digital.
Having a QR code or intranet link as backup is fine, but the main thing is that the paper version is easy to read and kept up to date.

For training, it helps if the checklist in A2 looks the same in print and on screen.
I support the mixed approach: printed for day-to-day use, digital for quick updates and for people who are off-site.
We should just make sure there is a simple way to check that the printed version is the latest one, maybe a version number and date at the bottom of each T8 one-pager.

No objections from me. Having both printed and digital versions also helps if we ever need to share the checklist with external partners during a joint drill.
We just need to coordinate with whoever manages the intranet so that the digital A2 and T8 files are in a clearly labelled crisis communication section.
I am fine with recording the mixed approach as our decision for this project.

To close this thread: we have agreed that the v1 content of the on-site incident escalation checklist in A2 is approved, and that we will provide it both in printed form at key locations and as a digital, mobile-friendly version via intranet or QR code.
I will coordinate with security operations and IT to make sure T8 reflects this distribution plan and that legal and safety teams complete their checks under T3.
Any final comments, please add them today so we can move on to the media and channel strategy work.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on media holding statements, Q&A, and channel strategy.

messages.text:
I have uploaded a first batch of draft holding statements and Q&A entries into A3, covering the five priority scenarios.
Each scenario has: a short holding line, a slightly longer update for when we know more, and a set of likely questions with suggested answers.
In parallel, I have started mapping channels and approval flows in A5 and T7, but those are still rough.
Please review A3 with three questions in mind: 1) Is the language clear and calm, 2) Does it align with what on-site teams will actually know at each stage, and 3) Are there any obvious legal or safety issues we should flag before sending this to legal for formal review.

I have gone through the A3 drafts.
Overall, the tone is measured and avoids speculation, which is good. For community relations, I would suggest we:
- Add a short reassurance line in each scenario about cooperation with authorities and commitment to safety
- Include one Q&A item per scenario about impact on neighbours or local traffic
On channels, the initial outline in A5 and T7 makes sense: internal alert first, then web and social, then press if needed. We just need to be explicit about who can trigger each step and how legal sign-off works in practice.

From the spokesperson side, I like that the A3 holding lines are short and do not overpromise.
A few practical points:
- For violence and medical emergencies, we should be very careful not to include any identifying details until families have been informed.
- For suspicious objects, we should avoid language that could cause panic, while still explaining why there is a cordon or disruption.
On A5 and T7, I would propose a default sequence per scenario: internal alert, update to security and operations, then external channels in a defined order. We can then adjust per incident, but at least we have a baseline.

I have read the A3 drafts with an eye on how they will be understood by staff and the general public.
The language is mostly straightforward, but there are a few phrases that might feel too technical under stress. I will suggest simpler alternatives directly in the document.
It would also help if each holding statement clearly states what is known, what is not yet known, and what people should do or not do. That structure is easy to explain in training.
Once we agree on the final wording, I can incorporate some of these examples into T6 so staff can practise delivering them in role plays.

Looking at A3 from the guard point of view, the holding lines seem fine, but I want to be sure they match what we are allowed to say on site.
In A2 and T3 we tell guards not to share details with bystanders or media and to refer questions to the spokesperson.
Maybe we can add a short reminder in A3 that these statements are for designated spokespeople only, and that guards should not try to repeat them from memory.
That way there is no confusion about who uses these texts.

Thanks for the feedback so far.
I have updated A3 to:
- Add a reassurance line and a neighbour impact Q&A per scenario
- Clarify that these texts are for designated spokespeople
- Simplify some of the more technical phrases
On A5 and T7, I have drafted a default channel sequence per scenario: internal alert (email or SMS), intranet update, social media post, web update, and press statement if needed.
Before we lock anything, I would like to agree on which holding statement in A3 should be the default for each scenario, so that spokespeople know which one to reach for first.

For each scenario in A3, I suggest we pick the shortest, most neutral holding line as the default.
For example:
- Violence: the line that confirms an incident, notes that security and emergency services are responding, and avoids any detail on individuals.
- Fire/smoke: the line that confirms an alarm and evacuation, and states that the cause is under investigation.
- Suspicious object: the line that explains there is a precautionary cordon without naming the object.
- Medical emergency: the line that acknowledges a medical incident and respects privacy.
- Police presence: the line that confirms cooperation with authorities without commenting on their investigation.
If everyone agrees, we can mark these as 'default' in A3 so they are easy to find.

I agree with that approach. The shorter, neutral lines are also less likely to cause issues if translated quickly or quoted out of context.
For community relations, it is important that the default lines do not sound defensive or dismissive. The ones you pointed to in A3 strike a good balance.
I support marking these as the default holding statements for each scenario.

From a training perspective, having one clearly marked default line per scenario in A3 will make it much easier to practise with spokespeople and managers.
I will use those default lines as the base examples in T6 and in any role plays we design.
I am comfortable with the selection you outlined and support recording them as the defaults.

I have now tagged the agreed lines in A3 as 'default' for each of the five scenarios.
On the channel strategy in A5 and T7, I have fleshed out the approval flow per channel: internal alerts approved by operations, web and social posts approved by PR with legal input for sensitive cases, and press statements approved by PR plus senior management.
Before we call this final, I would like to confirm that this flow is workable in a 24/7 context, especially for nights and weekends.

For 24/7 coverage, we need to be sure that there is always someone reachable who can approve external messages.
I suggest we define a small on-call pool for PR and legal, and list their contacts in A8. For low-severity incidents, the on-call PR person could approve social and web updates alone, using pre-cleared language from A3. For higher-severity cases, they would still try to reach legal and senior management, but the default is that we do not wait indefinitely if there is a clear safety need to communicate.
If we capture this logic in A5 and T7, I think the flow will be workable.

That makes sense. We already have an informal on-call rotation; we can formalise it in A8 and link it to the approval steps in A5 and T7.
For low-severity incidents, using pre-cleared A3 language without waiting for full legal review is reasonable, as long as we stick to the default lines and avoid adding extra detail.
I am comfortable approving the multi-channel strategy and approval flow on that basis, subject to legal confirming the on-call arrangement.

To summarise this thread:
- We have selected and tagged one default holding statement per scenario in A3.
- We have agreed on a multi-channel strategy in A5 and T7 with a clear approval flow, including an on-call arrangement to support 24/7 operations, to be validated with legal.
I will now send A3 and the relevant parts of A5 and T7 to legal for formal review, and update A8 with the proposed on-call contacts.
If there are no objections, we can record these as our decisions for this phase.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize internal briefing templates and training approach.

messages.text:
I have drafted the internal staff briefing templates in A4 and the first version of the training session content for security and front-line staff under T5 and T6.
For A4, there is a short briefing note template per scenario plus a generic template for follow-up updates. Each has sections for: what happened, what we know and do not know, what staff should do, and who to contact with questions.
For T6, I have outlined a 60-minute session: 10 minutes overview, 30 minutes scenario walk-throughs, 15 minutes role play, 5 minutes Q&A.
Please review with two questions in mind: 1) Is the tone and format of A4 appropriate for non-specialist staff, and 2) Does the T6 session plan feel realistic for your teams.

I have reviewed the A4 templates.
The structure is clear and matches the way we have framed the scenarios elsewhere. I particularly like the explicit 'what you should do' section, which will help reduce confusion.
A couple of suggestions:
- Add a short reminder in each template that staff should not share internal updates externally.
- Include a line about where to find the latest version of the playbook (A1) and the on-site checklist (A2).
On T6, the 60-minute plan looks workable. I would recommend that at least one spokesperson or PR person joins each session to handle questions about media and external messaging.

From the guard side, the A4 templates are easy to read. The bullet points help.
One thing: in the 'what happened' section, it might be better to avoid too much detail about how the incident started, especially for fights or medical issues. Maybe keep it more general so people do not start blaming each other.
For the T6 session, 60 minutes is ok, but we will need options for night shifts and weekends. Some guards may not be able to attend live sessions during the day.

I have checked A4 and T6 from a communications and risk angle.
The tone in A4 is calm and avoids speculation, which is good. I support adding the reminders 286680 mentioned about not sharing internally circulated information externally.
For T6, I suggest we include a short segment on why consistent messaging matters, linking back to A3 and A5, so staff understand the bigger picture.
In terms of format, I would lean toward a mixed approach: live sessions for key sites and roles, plus a recorded version for others who cannot attend.

From a community relations perspective, the A4 templates strike the right balance between transparency and caution.
I would only add that, where relevant, we include a short note about support resources for staff after serious incidents.
On training format, I agree with a mixed model: live sessions where possible, supported by a recording and perhaps a short written summary for those who prefer to read.
We should also think about how often we repeat the training, especially for new hires.

Thanks for the feedback.
I have updated A4 to:
- Add a reminder not to share internal updates externally
- Include a reference to where to find A1 and A2
- Soften some of the 'what happened' wording to avoid blame
- Add a short note on support resources after serious incidents
For T6, I have added a 5-minute segment on why consistent messaging matters, linking to A3 and A5, and a note that a spokesperson or PR representative should join each live session.
Before we call A4 final, can you confirm that the tone now feels right for your teams

I have re-read the updated A4 templates.
The tone is now consistent, clear, and aligned with the rest of the playbook. The reminders about not sharing externally and the references to A1 and A2 are helpful.
From my side, I am comfortable treating this version of A4 as the agreed format and tone for internal briefings.
We can still refine specific briefings later, but the template itself looks solid.

The updated A4 reads well to me. It is straightforward and does not point fingers.
I think guards and other staff will understand it without needing extra explanation.
I am ok with using this template for briefings during incidents.

The latest A4 version looks good from my side as well. It is consistent with A3 and A5 and should be easy to adapt per incident.
On training format, I support the mixed model you outlined: live 60-minute sessions where feasible, plus a recorded version and a short written summary.
We should also plan at least one joint dry run with PR or spokesperson present, as required by T6 and T9, to test the flow before we roll it out widely.

I agree with both points: A4 is ready to use, and a mixed training format is the most practical.
For scheduling under T9, we might start with a small number of pilot sessions at high-risk sites, then expand based on feedback.
We should also capture attendance so we know who has been trained and who still needs a session or to watch the recording.

To make this explicit: we are proposing a mixed training format for T6 and T9.
- Live 60-minute sessions for key sites and roles, co-facilitated by me and a PR or spokesperson
- A recorded version of the session for those who cannot attend live
- A short written summary of key points for quick reference
If everyone is comfortable with this, we can record it as our agreed training approach and start scheduling pilot sessions.

I support the mixed training approach you outlined.
It gives us enough flexibility for different shifts while still keeping a consistent core message.
Let us record that as the agreed format and move ahead with planning the first pilot sessions under T9.

The mixed format works for guards. Some will be able to join live, others will need the recording.
If we can schedule at least one live session per main shift, that would help.
I am ok with this being our training plan.

Great, then to close this thread:
- We have approved the internal staff briefing template format and tone in A4.
- We have agreed on a mixed training format under T6 and T9: live sessions plus recording and written summary.
I will now finalise T5 and T6 based on this, and start drafting a schedule for pilot sessions in T9.
Any last comments, please add them today so we can keep momentum.

threads.thread_goal: Close out project with review process and distribution plan.

messages.text:
We are approaching the deadline for the Crisis Communication Playbook v1.
In A1, I have assembled the latest versions of all sections: scenarios and escalation, internal briefings, media and channel strategy, and the post-incident review outline.
For this thread, we need to confirm that we are ready for rollout and align on: 1) the post-incident review and improvement process (T10 and A7), and 2) how we will distribute the final playbook and checklists to stakeholders (T12).
Please share any remaining gaps you see in A1 or A7, and how you suggest we handle distribution in practice.

I have reviewed A1 and the draft A7.
A1 looks complete for v1, with all the agreed sections and references to A2, A3, A4, A5, and A6.
For A7 and T10, I propose a simple post-incident review process:
- A short debrief within 48 hours with key roles (security, operations, PR, spokesperson)
- A more detailed review within two weeks using a standard template
- Clear actions assigned, with deadlines and owners, and updates to A1 and related artifacts as needed
We should also specify who is responsible for triggering the review, probably operations or PR depending on the incident type.

From a community relations angle, A1 and A7 cover the main points.
In A7, I would add one specific question about external perception: what did neighbours, media, or online comments focus on, and how did our messages land
This will help us refine A3 and A5 over time.
On distribution under T12, I suggest we:
- Share A1 and A2 with all relevant internal teams via intranet and email
- Provide a shorter summary for external partners where needed, without sensitive internal details
- Make sure senior management receives a brief overview of key changes and expectations.

Looking at A1 and A7 from a learning perspective, the review process in T10 should also capture what worked well, not just what went wrong.
I would add to A7:
- A short section on positive examples to repeat
- A question about whether staff felt they had the right tools (A2, A4, A6)
This will feed directly into updates to training content in T6 and future drills in T9.
For distribution under T12, we should also plan a short internal announcement that explains why the playbook matters and how staff can access it.

From the guard side, A1 looks good. The links to A2 and the checklists are clear.
For A7, it would help if the review template includes a simple section where guards can say what was confusing in the moment, for example radio codes, who to call, or where people were supposed to go.
On distribution, we need to make sure printed copies of the key parts (A2 and the quick-reference pages) actually reach the control rooms and posts, not just stay on email.

Thanks for the inputs.
I have updated A7 to include:
- A 48-hour quick debrief and a two-week detailed review
- A question on external perception and community feedback
- A section on what worked well and what to repeat
- A prompt for frontline staff feedback, including guards
This should satisfy T10 and give us a clear path to improve A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, and A6 over time.
On T12, I propose we define a distribution list in A8 and use that as the source of truth for who gets what.

The updated A7 looks good and aligns with what we discussed.
For T12, using A8 as the base for the distribution list makes sense. We can tag each contact with what they should receive: full A1, checklists A2, internal templates A4, drill materials A6, etc.
I can take the lead on drafting the internal announcement and a short note for senior management summarising the playbook and expectations.

I am happy with the A7 updates.
On distribution under T12, for external partners we should only share what is necessary: perhaps a high-level overview of A1 and selected parts of A6 for joint drills, but not internal escalation details.
I can help identify which community partners should receive that summary and coordinate with them once the internal rollout is complete.

The revised A7 works well from a learning standpoint.
For T12, I suggest we also include in the internal announcement a reminder about the upcoming training sessions and where to find the recording and summary once available.
That way, staff see the playbook and the training as part of the same effort, not separate initiatives.

The A7 template looks fine to me. The questions are clear enough that guards can answer them without a lot of writing.
On distribution, please make sure that whoever is responsible for each site confirms when they have printed and posted the latest A2 checklists. Maybe we can add a simple tick box in T12 for that.

Based on the feedback, I think we can say that the post-incident review process in A7 and T10 is agreed for v1.
For distribution under T12, here is the plan I propose:
- Publish A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, and A7 on the intranet in a dedicated crisis communication section
- Use A8 to define who receives which parts by email
- Ensure printed A2 and quick-reference pages are delivered to control rooms and key posts, with confirmation tracked in T12
- Send an internal announcement and a short note to senior management summarising the playbook and training plan
If there are no objections, I will proceed on this basis.

I support that plan.
I will take care of the internal announcement and the senior management note, and help finalise the distribution list in A8.
With that, I believe we can consider the playbook ready for v1 rollout, pending any minor edits from legal.

Thanks all.
We will treat A1 as the v1 Crisis Communication Playbook, with A7 and T10 defining how we improve it after each incident or drill, and T12 guiding distribution.
I will coordinate with operations, security, PR, and training to make sure the rollout steps are completed before the next quarterly safety drill.
If any issues come up during legal review or the first drills, we will capture them using the A7 template and feed them into the next version.
